script.opening: "My mate’s mum found some vapes and a few pills in my bag and made a massive deal of it. Honestly it’s nothing — everyone at school does it, it’s no big deal. I only came because I was made to. You’re not going to tell my parents or get me in trouble, are you?"

facts.text: His mum booked it after the friend’s mum rang her. Mum knows about the vapes and pills; she is waiting in the car. Kai is on the video call alone in his bedroom.
Lives with Mum and younger sister. Dad left 2 years ago; sees him "now and then". Rows with Mum about curfew. "Fine. Normal."
Year 10. "School’s all right." Grades dropped this year; had two detentions for lateness. Used to play football; stopped last season. Hangs out with mates at the park and an older lad’s flat.

facts.topic: Drugs and alcohol (if asked without judgement)
facts.text: Vapes most days — "everyone does". The pills were "just something going round" from an older lad, Dee (19); took half of one twice, "maybe with a drink". Doesn’t know what they are. Drinks cider at weekends, 3–4 cans. Has tried cannabis a few times.

Dee gave him the pills "for free" and keeps offering more. If asked whether anyone has asked him to carry, sell or hold anything: "No. It’s not like that." No extra phone, no unexplained money, not threatened, never missing overnight. Not been hurt by anyone. If asked about online contacts: nothing worrying.
Has a girlfriend; "not really" sexually active — declines to say more. Mood "I’m all right"; sleeps late, tired. No self-harm, no suicidal thoughts.
No medicines, no allergies, mild asthma as a child.

Guarded, monosyllabic, slouching. Open up a little only if the doctor explains confidentiality honestly and talks to you, not at you. If lectured, shut down ("Whatever"). If the doctor asks about older friends, mention Dee; deny being asked to carry anything. Admit a mate was sick after the pills only if asked whether anything has gone wrong. Take harm-reduction advice about the pills seriously.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he is quietly uneasy that Dee keeps giving him free stuff, and frightened after a friend was sick on the pills; mostly afraid his mum will find out about the cider and the cannabis.
ice.expectations: "For you to say it’s fine and not tell my mum."

cues: "You’re not going to tell my parents, are you?" — confidentiality to explain honestly, with its limits.
"Just something going round" — unknown pills; harm-reduction message.
"An older lad" (if friends are explored) — possible criminal exploitation to screen for.

checkpoints.text: Builds RAPPORT and engages the teenager DIRECTLY and non-judgementally, rather than lecturing, recognising he attended reluctantly

Clarifies CONFIDENTIALITY honestly up front, in line with GMC 0–18 years guidance — confidential unless there is a risk of serious harm to him/others (then information may be shared/safeguarding, telling him first where safe) — rather than promising blanket secrecy
Takes a structured HEADSS psychosocial assessment with a non-judgemental substance history (what/how much/route/frequency/context/funding/other drugs/alcohol)
Actively screens RISK and SAFEGUARDING — child criminal/sexual EXPLOITATION (county lines), abuse/neglect, mental-health/self-harm, dependence, risky behaviours

Assesses and records GILLICK competence and provides HARM-REDUCTION/motivational advice (unknown pills and counterfeit tablets containing nitazenes; not alone, no alcohol, 999 if someone can’t be woken; vapes illegal to sell to under-18s; his goals) rather than moralising
Signposts/refers to young people’s SUBSTANCE-MISUSE (NICE NG64) and mental-health services (self-harm per NICE NG225), and involves parents/safeguarding where proportionate and in his interests
Explains any information-sharing or safeguarding step to him before acting, keeping him engaged and informed rather than feeling betrayed, and agrees a plan he is willing to follow

Reaches a safe, supportive plan with appropriate safeguarding action, harm-reduction, signposting, competence/confidentiality handled correctly, and follow-up — engaging the teenager, not lecturing or breaching trust unnecessarily

worked.txt: "Thanks for coming in, even if you were made to — I’m not here to tell you off or get you in trouble. I’d genuinely just like to understand what’s going on from your side. Is that okay?"

"Let me be straight about confidentiality, because it matters: what you tell me stays between us — I won’t automatically tell your parents. The only exception is if I’m worried you or someone else is at serious risk of harm, when I might need to involve others to keep you safe. I’ll always try to talk to you first. Can I ask — who made you come today, and do your parents know about this?"

"Tell me a bit about things generally — home, school, what you do for fun — and then about the vapes and pills: what are they, how often, who with, and how do you get them? No judgement, I just need the real picture."

"A couple of important questions: where do the pills come from, and does anyone older give them to you or ask you to carry or sell things? Do you owe anyone money? And how’s your mood — ever felt like harming yourself?"

"Can I share a couple of facts, and you decide what to do with them? Pills that don’t come from a pharmacy can contain something completely different — some fake tablets in the UK have had very strong opioids in them. So never take them alone, don’t mix them with alcohol, and if someone can’t be woken, call 999. There’s a young people’s service that’s confidential and really helpful — I can refer you. What would YOU want to change, if anything?"

"If I’m worried about your safety I’ll be honest with you about what I need to do. It’s also worth having a trusted adult in your corner — we can think about that together. Come back any time; you’re not in trouble with me."

f.learning: Substance misuse in a teenager is an ADOLESCENT consultation where engagement and safeguarding matter as much as the drugs. Build RAPPORT and engage the young person directly and non-judgementally — a lecture loses them. Clarify CONFIDENTIALITY honestly at the outset, seeing the young person alone: under GMC 0–18 years guidance they are owed the same duty of confidentiality as adults, and information is shared without consent only where needed to protect them or others from a risk of serious harm (safeguarding), telling them first where safe; being upfront builds trust and is more honest than promising blanket secrecy. Take a structured HEADSS psychosocial assessment — Home, Education/employment, Activities, Drugs (and alcohol/vaping: what, how much, route, frequency, context, who with, how funded), Sexuality/relationships, and Suicide/self-harm/mood/Safety — framing the substance use within the whole of the young person’s life. Critically, assess RISK and SAFEGUARDING: child criminal/sexual EXPLOITATION (county lines — unexplained money/items, older "friends", going missing, being recruited to carry or sell, owing money/debt bondage), abuse/neglect, mental-health/self-harm, dependence and risky behaviours — questions about where substances come from, who supplies them and any debts can reveal exploitation — and involve safeguarding where indicated (practice safeguarding lead and children’s social care, Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023; Home Office county lines guidance). Assess and record GILLICK competence, provide HARM-REDUCTION and motivational advice (honest information without scare-mongering, exploring the young person’s own goals — unidentified illicit pills may be counterfeit and contain nitazenes, so not alone, not with alcohol, 999 if someone can’t be woken; selling vapes to under-18s is illegal) rather than moralising, screen mood and self-harm (NICE NG225), and signpost/refer to young people’s substance-misuse (NICE NG64) and mental-health services, involving parents/a trusted adult and safeguarding where proportionate and in the young person’s interests. The skill is engaging the adolescent, handling confidentiality correctly, HEADSS/safeguarding (especially exploitation), harm reduction not lecturing, and appropriate signposting/referral.

knowledge.guideline: [1] GMC 0–18 years: guidance for all doctors (2007, updated 2018) · [2] NICE NG64 Drug misuse prevention: targeted interventions (2017) · [3] HM Government Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023) · [4] Home Office Criminal exploitation of children and vulnerable adults: county lines guidance (2018) · [5] NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (2022) · [6] Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA (1985)
knowledge.summary: A 15-year-old caught with vapes and unknown pills needs an adolescent consultation, not a lecture. Explain confidentiality honestly at the start, see him on his own, and use a HEADSS framework to understand his life and his use. Screen actively for exploitation (county lines, debt, older suppliers), abuse, self-harm and dependence. Assess and record his competence. Give honest harm-reduction information, offer a confidential young people’s substance service, encourage a trusted adult, and share information without consent only when there is a risk of serious harm, telling him first where safe.

points.t: Young people are owed the same duty of confidentiality as adults [1]. Information can be shared without consent where it is needed to protect the young person or others from a risk of serious harm, such as abuse or exploitation [1,3]. Say this at the start rather than promising secrecy, and tell him before sharing unless that would increase the risk.

A young person under 16 can consent to advice and treatment if they understand what is involved (Gillick competence [6]). Assess and record it. Encourage involvement of parents or another trusted adult, but do not make it a condition of help [1].

Home, Education or employment, Activities, Drugs (what, how much, how often, route, where, who with, how it is paid for; alcohol, vaping and tobacco), Sexuality and relationships, Suicide, self-harm, mood and Safety. It places substance use in the context of his whole life and uncovers risk.

County lines guidance [4]: warning signs include unexplained money, phones or clothes, older ‘friends’, going missing, being asked to carry or sell, and owing money. Also consider abuse, neglect and sexual exploitation. Act through the practice safeguarding lead and local children’s social care where there is a concern [3].

Pills bought illicitly may not contain what the seller claims: UK public health alerts have described counterfeit benzodiazepine tablets containing potent synthetic opioids (nitazenes). Advise against using alone or mixing with alcohol or other drugs, and to call 999 if someone cannot be woken. Sale of vapes to under-18s is illegal in the UK and unregulated vapes may contain other substances. Screen mood and self-harm [5].

NG64 [2] recommends assessing vulnerability to drug misuse during routine GP contacts and offering targeted support, such as referral to specialist young people’s services, for those at risk or already experimenting. Arrange follow-up rather than a single conversation.

dg.d: Acknowledges he was made to come; open, non-judgemental invitation to give his side.
HEADSS: home, school, activities, friends, sexual relationships, mood and safety.
No examination needed; considers vital signs or examination only if he were intoxicated or unwell.
Experimental use versus regular or dependent use; linked mental health problems; exploitation.
Exploitation, debt, abuse, self-harm and suicide risk screened; overdose risk from unknown pills.
Occasional use of unknown pills and daily vaping, with no disclosed safeguarding concern today.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Honest harm reduction; young people’s substance service offered as his choice; trusted adult encouraged.
Confidentiality and its limit explained up front; Gillick competence assessed and recorded; safeguarding lead if concern emerges.
Follow-up in about two weeks; safety-net for low mood, exploitation and overdose; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up “I don’t know what they are” and “maybe with a drink” as risk cues.
His idea (no big deal), concern (parents told; trouble), expectation (secrecy).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — he is quietly uneasy that Dee keeps giving him free stuff, and frightened after a friend was sick on the pills; mostly afraid his mum will find out about the cider and the cannabis — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Kai, I’m Dr Morgan. Thanks for coming in, even though it sounds like it wasn’t your idea. I’m not here to tell you off. I’d like to hear your side.

My mate’s mum found some vapes and a few pills in my bag and made a massive deal of it. Honestly, it’s nothing. Everyone at school does it. You’re not going to tell my parents or get me in trouble, are you?

Fair question, so I’ll be straight with you. What you tell me stays between us, and I won’t ring your parents after you leave. The one exception is if I’m worried that you or someone else is at risk of serious harm. Then I might need to involve other people to keep you safe, and I’d talk to you first. Does that make sense?
model.why: Honest confidentiality with its limit, stated before disclosure

model.text: I suppose.
Can I get a picture of your life generally first? How are things at home?
Fine. Normal.
And school: how’s it going, and what do you do outside school, who do you hang around with?
School’s all right. I just hang out with my mates.
Tell me about the vapes and the pills. How often do you vape? And the pills: do you know what they are?
I vape most days, like everyone. The pills were just something going round. I don’t really know what they are.
Have you taken any? How many, how often, and with anything else, like alcohol or weed?
Only a couple of times. Maybe with a drink.
Where do they come from, and how are they paid for? Has anyone older given them to you, asked you to carry or sell things, or said you owe them?
model.why: Actively screens criminal exploitation and debt (county lines)

model.text: No. It’s not like that.
Okay. If that ever changes, you can tell me and it won’t get you in trouble with me. Has anyone ever pressured you into anything sexual, or hurt you?
No.
How has your mood been lately? Have you ever felt so low you’ve hurt yourself or thought about ending your life?
No, I’m all right.
What do you make of it all? What’s the bit that worries you most about today?
That it turns into a massive thing and my parents find out. I don’t think it’s a big deal.
Thanks for being honest, that helps. Can I tell you a couple of facts, and you decide what you do with them?
model.why: Asks permission; motivational rather than lecturing

model.text: Go on.

The pills are the part that worries me. When pills aren’t from a pharmacy, nobody knows what’s in them. Some fake tablets sold as things like Xanax in the UK have turned out to contain very strong opioids, and young people have died. So if you’re ever around them: don’t take them alone, don’t mix them with drink, and if a friend can’t be woken, call 999 straight away.
model.why: Honest, specific harm reduction without scare tactics

model.text: With vaping, the ones sold to under-18s aren’t legal, so they’re not checked, and some have had other things in them. What would you want to change, if anything?
Maybe the pills. I didn’t know that about them. The vaping’s fine.
That’s a good call. There’s a young people’s service locally that’s confidential and doesn’t lecture. I can refer you, or give you the details to contact them yourself. Which would you prefer?
model.why: Offers youth substance service; his choice

model.text: Give me the details. I’ll think about it.

You’ve clearly understood what we’ve talked about, so you can make these decisions with me. Is there an adult you trust who you could talk to about this? I won’t tell your parents, but having someone on your side helps.
model.why: Gillick competence assessed and recorded; encourages a trusted adult without coercion

model.text: Maybe. I’ll see.

Fair enough. Come back and see me in a couple of weeks, just to catch up. Before then, if you feel really low, if anyone pressures you or says you owe them, or if something goes wrong after taking something, get help straight away: call 999 in an emergency, or come to us. Can you tell me the main things you’ll take away?
model.why: Follow-up; safety-net for mood, exploitation and overdose; teach-back

model.text: Don’t take pills you don’t know, not on my own, not with drink. Call 999 if someone won’t wake up. Check out that service. Come back in two weeks.
Spot on. Thanks for talking to me, Kai. You’re not in trouble with me.
model.why: Ends on trust to keep the door open

social.t: Normalisation (“everyone does it”) is common. School and friendship pressures shape use; education staff may be part of support if he agrees.
Involving a trusted adult improves safety, but the choice of whom rests with him unless there is a safeguarding need.

legal.t: Gillick competence allows a young person under 16 to consent to advice and treatment. GMC 0–18 years guidance supports confidentiality, with disclosure where there is a risk of serious harm.
Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023): concerns about abuse or exploitation, including county lines, are referred to local children’s social care, usually via the practice safeguarding lead.
Selling nicotine vapes to under-18s is illegal in the UK.

professional.t: Record the competence assessment, the advice given, and the reasons for any decision to share or not share information.
If uncertain whether a concern meets the threshold, discuss with the practice safeguarding lead without delay.

community.t: Local young people’s drug and alcohol services are confidential and accept self-referral. School nurses and youth services can also support him.

redFlags: Owing money, older suppliers, carrying or selling, unexplained cash or phones, going missing: criminal exploitation
Low mood, self-harm or suicidal thoughts (NG225)
Unknown pills, use alone or with alcohol: overdose risk
Daily or escalating use, withdrawal: dependence
ice: Idea: no big deal, everyone does it
Concern: parents told; getting into trouble
Expectation: that it will be kept secret

playbook.diagnosis: “Occasional use of unknown pills and regular vaping, with no safeguarding concern disclosed today, which needs harm reduction and follow-up.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The vaping is mainly a nicotine habit. The pills are the bigger risk: when they don’t come from a pharmacy, nobody knows what’s in them, so one bad batch can be dangerous.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried I’d tell your parents. I won’t, unless I’m worried about serious harm, and I’d talk to you first.”
management.psychosocial: Keep the relationship; give him choices; encourage a trusted adult.
sharedPlan: Confidentiality and its limit explained; competence recorded
Harm reduction: unknown pills, not alone, not with alcohol, 999
safetyNet: Low mood, self-harm thoughts, pressure or debt: contact the practice or 999 in an emergency

pitfalls.intro: The marks sit in relating to a reluctant teenager: honest confidentiality, no lecture, and still asking the hard questions about exploitation and self-harm.

items.fail: Promising total secrecy, or threatening to tell his parents.
items.why: Both are inaccurate and damage trust.
items.fix: State confidentiality and its serious-harm limit at the start.
Ask permission, give specific facts, and ask what he wants to change.

items.fail: Not asking where the pills came from or whether he owes anyone.
items.why: County lines exploitation is easily missed.
items.fix: Ask about suppliers, carrying, selling and debt.

items.why: Substance use and self-harm often coexist.
items.fix: Ask directly and follow NG225 if positive.
Explain counterfeit pills, not using alone or with alcohol, and calling 999.

items.fail: Treating it as a one-off conversation.
items.why: Trust and change build over time.
items.fix: Offer a service and a review in about two weeks; record competence.

Home, school, activities, then the vapes and pills: what, how often, with what, where from, how paid for. Exploitation, abuse, mood and self-harm.
His view and his fear of his parents finding out.
Permission first; unknown pills and nitazenes; not alone, not with alcohol, 999; vapes; his own goals; youth service offered.
Competence recorded; trusted adult; review in two weeks; safety-net; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Lectures him about drugs; promises total secrecy, or says his parents must be told; never asks where the pills came from; misses mood and self-harm.
wordPics.pass: Explains confidentiality honestly, takes a HEADSS history, screens exploitation and self-harm, gives harm-reduction advice and signposts a young people’s service.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: asks permission before giving information; gives specific, credible advice about counterfeit pills and overdose; lets him choose the next step; assesses and records competence; encourages a trusted adult without coercion; arranges follow-up to build the relationship.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, nothing you say leaves this room.”
avoid.instead: “It stays between us unless I’m worried about serious harm, and then I’d talk to you first.”
avoid.why: Blanket secrecy cannot be kept and breaks trust later [GMC 0–18].

avoid.dont: “Drugs will ruin your life. You need to stop.”
avoid.instead: “Can I share a couple of facts, and you decide what to do with them?”
avoid.why: Lecturing disengages teenagers; motivational, honest information works better.

avoid.dont: “I’ll have to let your parents know about this.”
avoid.instead: “Is there an adult you trust who you could talk to? I won’t tell them without your say-so unless you’re at serious risk.”
avoid.why: A competent 15-year-old is owed confidentiality; parents are involved by consent unless there is a risk of serious harm.

points.t: Young people are owed the same duty of confidentiality as adults [1]. Information can be shared without consent where it is needed to protect the young person or others from a risk of serious harm, such as abuse or exploitation [1,3]. Say this at the start rather than promising secrecy, and tell him before sharing unless that would increase the risk.

A young person under 16 can consent to advice and treatment if they understand what is involved (Gillick competence [6]). Assess and record it. Encourage involvement of parents or another trusted adult, but do not make it a condition of help [1].

Home, Education or employment, Activities, Drugs (what, how much, how often, route, where, who with, how it is paid for; alcohol, vaping and tobacco), Sexuality and relationships, Suicide, self-harm, mood and Safety. It places substance use in the context of his whole life and uncovers risk.

County lines guidance [4]: warning signs include unexplained money, phones or clothes, older ‘friends’, going missing, being asked to carry or sell, and owing money. Also consider abuse, neglect and sexual exploitation. Act through the practice safeguarding lead and local children’s social care where there is a concern [3].

Pills bought illicitly may not contain what the seller claims: UK public health alerts have described counterfeit benzodiazepine tablets containing potent synthetic opioids (nitazenes). Advise against using alone or mixing with alcohol or other drugs, and to call 999 if someone cannot be woken. Sale of vapes to under-18s is illegal in the UK and unregulated vapes may contain other substances. Screen mood and self-harm [5].

NG64 [2] recommends assessing vulnerability to drug misuse during routine GP contacts and offering targeted support, such as referral to specialist young people’s services, for those at risk or already experimenting. Arrange follow-up rather than a single conversation.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Acknowledges he was made to come; open, non-judgemental invitation to give his side.
HEADSS: home, school, activities, friends, sexual relationships, mood and safety.
Picks up “I don’t know what they are” and “maybe with a drink” as risk cues.
His idea (no big deal), concern (parents told; trouble), expectation (secrecy).
No examination needed; considers vital signs or examination only if he were intoxicated or unwell.
Experimental use versus regular or dependent use; linked mental health problems; exploitation.
Exploitation, debt, abuse, self-harm and suicide risk screened; overdose risk from unknown pills.
Occasional use of unknown pills and daily vaping, with no disclosed safeguarding concern today.
Honest harm reduction; young people’s substance service offered as his choice; trusted adult encouraged.
Confidentiality and its limit explained up front; Gillick competence assessed and recorded; safeguarding lead if concern emerges.
Follow-up in about two weeks; safety-net for low mood, exploitation and overdose; teach-back.

social.t: Normalisation (“everyone does it”) is common. School and friendship pressures shape use; education staff may be part of support if he agrees.
Involving a trusted adult improves safety, but the choice of whom rests with him unless there is a safeguarding need.

legal.t: Gillick competence allows a young person under 16 to consent to advice and treatment. GMC 0–18 years guidance supports confidentiality, with disclosure where there is a risk of serious harm.
Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023): concerns about abuse or exploitation, including county lines, are referred to local children’s social care, usually via the practice safeguarding lead.
Selling nicotine vapes to under-18s is illegal in the UK.

professional.t: Record the competence assessment, the advice given, and the reasons for any decision to share or not share information.
If uncertain whether a concern meets the threshold, discuss with the practice safeguarding lead without delay.

community.t: Local young people’s drug and alcohol services are confidential and accept self-referral. School nurses and youth services can also support him.

redFlags: Owing money, older suppliers, carrying or selling, unexplained cash or phones, going missing: criminal exploitation
Low mood, self-harm or suicidal thoughts (NG225)
Unknown pills, use alone or with alcohol: overdose risk
Daily or escalating use, withdrawal: dependence
ice: Idea: no big deal, everyone does it
Concern: parents told; getting into trouble
Expectation: that it will be kept secret

management.reflectIce: “You were worried I’d tell your parents. I won’t, unless I’m worried about serious harm, and I’d talk to you first.”
management.psychosocial: Keep the relationship; give him choices; encourage a trusted adult.
sharedPlan: Confidentiality and its limit explained; competence recorded
Harm reduction: unknown pills, not alone, not with alcohol, 999
safetyNet: Low mood, self-harm thoughts, pressure or debt: contact the practice or 999 in an emergency

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The marks sit in relating to a reluctant teenager: honest confidentiality, no lecture, and still asking the hard questions about exploitation and self-harm.

items.fail: Promising total secrecy, or threatening to tell his parents.
items.why: Both are inaccurate and damage trust.
items.fix: State confidentiality and its serious-harm limit at the start.
Ask permission, give specific facts, and ask what he wants to change.

items.fail: Not asking where the pills came from or whether he owes anyone.
items.why: County lines exploitation is easily missed.
items.fix: Ask about suppliers, carrying, selling and debt.

items.why: Substance use and self-harm often coexist.
items.fix: Ask directly and follow NG225 if positive.
Explain counterfeit pills, not using alone or with alcohol, and calling 999.

items.fail: Treating it as a one-off conversation.
items.why: Trust and change build over time.
items.fix: Offer a service and a review in about two weeks; record competence.
